lead: A simulator, an emulator and an in-circuit debugger all let you watch and control target code, but they trade realism for visibility and cost. A simulator runs a model of the microcontroller (MCU) on your laptop. An emulator uses hardware that replaces or mimics the MCU. An in-circuit debugger (ICD) uses debug logic inside the real chip, reached through JTAG or SWD. You use these tools to find startup faults, inspect registers and memory, set breakpoints and step through code before or during board testing.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for executables and symbols, and Unit 3 for on-chip peripherals.

sections.h3: Simulator: the MCU as a host program

blocks.text: A simulator is a host program that models the microcontroller. It keeps a model of the CPU registers, condition flags, memory map, timers, interrupt controller and some peripherals. It loads the same executable and symbol file produced by the cross-toolchain (Chapter 6.2). No target board is needed. You can set breakpoints, single-step, read and write memory, watch variables, and inject UART bytes or ADC values. This makes it cheap and repeatable for checking startup code, control flow and arithmetic before hardware exists.

The model is not the chip. Peripheral behaviour is approximate, electrical faults do not appear, and instruction timing may ignore flash wait states, DMA contention or caches. A simulator can count instructions, but its clock is not the target clock. Use it for logic bugs, not for final timing or signal-integrity tests.

blocks.where: t<sub>sim</sub> is simulated execution time in seconds; N<sub>inst</sub> is the number of instructions executed; CPI is the average cycles per instruction; f<sub>CPU</sub> is the clock frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: An emulator uses hardware to stand in for the microcontroller. A pod contains a matching MCU or an FPGA that mimics the MCU internals. An emulator pod connects to the target socket (or a dedicated emulation header) so that it takes the place of the MCU. An in-circuit debugger, by contrast, needs only the small JTAG or SWD header on the board. Because the pod runs the code, the target board can keep its real connectors, sensors and power supply. Full in-circuit emulators replaced the CPU with a special bond-out chip; modern designs more often use on-chip debug logic already present in the MCU.

On-chip debug (OCD) reaches that logic through JTAG (Joint Test Action Group, a multi-wire test and debug port) or SWD (Serial Wire Debug, a two-wire ARM debug port). A probe connects the host to the chip. Basic operations are halt, run, single-step one instruction, set breakpoints, set watchpoints, read or write memory and program flash. A breakpoint stops before an instruction executes. A watchpoint stops when code reads or writes a chosen address. Trace records program flow without halting, using on-chip trace hardware; it is the tool for faults that disappear when the CPU stops. In ARM CoreSight chips the block that gives the probe access to the bus and memory is called the debug access port (DAP); the whole on-chip debug logic is usually just called the debug interface. Only a few universities go deeper into trace hardware.

Startup code is a common target. Break at the reset vector, then step through stack-pointer setup, clock configuration, copying initialized data from flash to SRAM, clearing .bss and calling main. A fault here often shows as a dead board with no output. JTAG also supports boundary scan, but that board-level test is Chapter 6.8.

sections.h3: Choosing the tool and its limits

blocks.text: Choose by the question you are asking. A simulator answers 'is the logic right?' An emulator answers 'how does the code behave with this board and bus?' In-circuit debug answers 'what is the real chip doing now?'

Real-time limits matter. Halting the CPU stops instruction execution. On most MCUs the timers, serial ports and watchdog keep running unless the debugger freezes them, so interrupts are serviced late and the watchdog can reset the board. Hardware breakpoints are few because they use comparator registers. Software breakpoints write a special instruction into memory, so they fail in ROM or flash unless the debugger can erase and rewrite the flash. Use trace or a spare pin for timing bugs, and use the simulator for long deterministic runs.

examples.question: A loop runs 1000 times. Each iteration executes 8 instructions. The target runs at 16 MHz with CPI (cycles per instruction) 1.5. Find the time from loop start to a breakpoint placed after the loop.
steps: Clock frequency = 16 MHz = 16,000,000 cycles per second.
examples.answer: The loop takes 12,000 cycles and 0.75 ms to reach the breakpoint after the loop.
examples.check:
loop_iterations = 1000
instructions_per_iteration = 8
cpi = 1.5
clock_hz = 16_000_000
cycles = loop_iterations * instructions_per_iteration * cpi
time_s = cycles / clock_hz
time_ms = time_s * 1000
print(int(cycles))
print(round(time_ms, 6))

traps: Simulator time is not target time. A simulator may count instructions correctly but miss flash wait states, DMA contention, cache misses or interrupt latency.
A software breakpoint needs writable memory. It fails in ROM or flash unless the debugger supports flash patching; a hardware breakpoint uses a comparator instead.
An emulator is hardware that replaces or mimics the MCU; a simulator is software on the host. The words are not interchangeable in an exam answer.
Halting the CPU for a breakpoint changes interrupt timing and can trigger the watchdog. Bugs that depend on real-time behaviour may need trace, not a halt.
JTAG debug and JTAG boundary scan share a port but do different jobs. Debug controls program execution; boundary scan tests board nets and pins, as in Chapter 6.8.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a simulator and an emulator?
quiz.a: A simulator is software on a host that models the MCU. An emulator is hardware that replaces or mimics the MCU and runs with the target board.

quiz.q: Name two transports used by on-chip debug.
Why can a software breakpoint fail in flash memory?
quiz.a: A software breakpoint replaces an instruction with a break instruction. Flash cannot be overwritten byte by byte during a run, and the debugger may lack flash patch support. A hardware breakpoint comparator avoids this.

quiz.q: Why does halting the CPU hide some real-time bugs?
quiz.a: Halting stops instruction execution; the peripherals and watchdog usually keep counting, so the bug that depends on interrupt latency or on the watchdog firing is lost. Trace runs without halting.

quiz.q: A loop runs 400 times, with 10 instructions per iteration, CPI 2 and clock 10 MHz. Find the cycles and the time to a breakpoint after the loop.
A debugger supports only two hardware breakpoints. You need to stop on a function entry, on a write to a variable, and also step through startup. What would you do?
quiz.a: Use one hardware breakpoint at reset or startup. After startup, move it to the function entry or the watchpoint. Use single-step or temporary software breakpoints in RAM for the rest. Hardware comparators are scarce, so plan their use.

quiz.q: Give one reason to use a simulator before an in-circuit debugger for startup code.
quiz.a: A simulator can step the reset vector, stack setup, memory copy and clearing with full visibility and no board, catching logic errors early. The in-circuit debugger then checks the real clock, flash and hardware. The simulator cannot test electrical behaviour.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, debug probes such as OpenOCD-compatible adapters drive JTAG or SWD from an IDE, and trace hardware captures program flow while the target runs. Continuous integration often runs unit tests on a simulator or a full-system model first, then on a hardware-in-loop bench. Search for 'OpenOCD', 'ARM CoreSight', 'serial-wire trace' and 'QEMU embedded' to go further.
